sentences.text: The assessment is being conducted with Margaret Doyle, who was referred by the hospital after a fall on March 3rd.
The fall resulted in a fractured left wrist, which required hospitalisation for four days on orthopaedic ward.
The assessment aims to understand how Margaret is managing daily life, identify difficulties, and explore what matters most to her, under the Care Act.
The assessment is not about placing Margaret in a care home; it is about supporting her to remain in her own home.
The visit was initially expected to take about an hour, but was extended due to Margaret’s willingness to share more about her situation.
Kevin Doyle, Margaret’s son, was present during parts of the assessment and provided additional perspectives on her needs and concerns.
Margaret has difficulty with mobility due to her fractured wrist and reliance on a walking frame.
She uses the frame indoors but sometimes holds onto furniture as a temporary measure, which is unsafe.
She has only walked a short distance since returning home, fearing another fall, and previously walked to the shops (about 10 minutes) before the fall.
Margaret struggles with stairs, using a rail on one side while going up and down, and sometimes sits on the floor to avoid using the rail.
She has a second rail on the stairs but lacks a second frame for upstairs.
She avoids baths due to difficulty getting out of the tub after a fall, preferring a strip wash at the sink.
She misses having a proper bath and washing her hair, which she used to do regularly.
Dressing takes up to an hour, with difficulty managing buttons, hooks, and tights, often wearing the same cardigan and elasticated trousers.
She occasionally stays in her nightclothes, admitting it happens on some days.
She uses pads for continence at night, having missed some bladder accidents due to rushing to the toilet.
Margaret values her independence and wants to remain in her own home for as long as possible.
She is deeply attached to her garden, especially Frank’s roses, and fears losing them if she moves.
She misses her social life, particularly the lunch club at St Michael’s, where she used to meet Joan and Pat.
She wants to regain confidence in her ability to cook and prepare meals, though she currently avoids the kitchen due to fear of another fall.
She expressed a desire to have a bath again and wash her hair properly, which she previously enjoyed as a nightly routine.
Margaret’s son, Kevin, has expressed concerns about her safety and suggested she might benefit from a sheltered flat or a bungalow.
Kevin also mentioned that Brenda next door has been a helpful neighbour, especially in emergencies.
Kevin has been helping with shopping and household tasks but admits he does more than he should.
Margaret’s daughter, Susan, visits regularly and is worried about her mother’s well-being, especially after Frank’s death.
Margaret has a strong desire to avoid being a burden on others and prefers to manage her own affairs.
Margaret has had three falls in the last six months, including a recent fall that resulted in a fractured wrist.
She has not been referred to a falls clinic or received a falls assessment from her GP.
She has not used a fall detection alarm or emergency pendant, despite Kevin mentioning it.
Margaret has admitted she is worried about falling again and fears losing independence.
There is a risk of further falls and injuries due to unsafe mobility, lack of assistive equipment, and unsafe home environment (e.g., rugs, stairs).
Margaret has disclosed that her grandson, Jordan, has been borrowing her bank card without her permission, leading to unauthorized withdrawals of approximately £600 over two months.
Kevin has heard rumors that Jordan may be involved in gambling and has taken his card to prevent further unauthorized transactions.
Margaret has denied any thoughts of self-harm or suicide, but has mentioned feeling low after Frank’s death and taking antidepressants.
Margaret has not been taking her blood pressure medication consistently, missing two doses in the last week.
The safeguarding team will be contacted to address the unauthorized withdrawals and ensure Margaret’s safety.
Margaret’s support network includes Kevin, who helps with shopping and household tasks, Brenda next door, and her daughter Susan.
Brenda is a frequent neighbour who checks on Margaret daily and has been a lifeline during emergencies.
Margaret misses her social life, particularly the lunch club at St Michael’s, where she used to meet friends regularly.
Margaret’s financial situation includes her state pension, Frank’s widow’s pension, and savings of approximately £9,000 in the building society.
She has not been receiving Attendance Allowance, despite meeting criteria for it.
Margaret’s grandson, Jordan, has been borrowing her bank card for unauthorized transactions, leading to financial concerns.
Kevin has agreed to cancel Margaret’s bank card and order a new one to prevent further unauthorized transactions.
Margaret will be referred to occupational therapy for a bath lift or board, a second rail on the stairs, and a second frame for upstairs.
A safeguarding adults referral will be made regarding unauthorized bank card withdrawals, with Margaret’s wishes prioritized.
Margaret will be referred for a fall detection alarm (Careline watch) to be fitted within ten days.
Margaret will be contacted by Dr Shah regarding a falls clinic referral, weight loss, continence service, and easier-to-open medication packs.
Kevin will take Margaret to the Midshire building society on Friday morning to cancel her bank card and order a new one.
Kevin will help Margaret fill out the Attendance Allowance form and financial assessment form.
Kevin will remove the rug in the hall this weekend.
Margaret will set her alarm clock for her morning medication.
A request for reablement support (short-term, daily visits for washing, dressing, meals, and medication) will be made, with a decision expected by the end of next week.
Margaret will be contacted on Monday to check on the bank card cancellation and to discuss next steps.
